tldr: We developed a simulator that eliminates nondeterminism from ROS 2 asynchronous communication using a lightweight coordination scheme with fixed I/O instants, enabling fast, parallel, and out-of-order execution based on dependencies known before the run.
overview:
ROS 2 is widely used in autonomous driving and robotics development. However, developers have long struggled with nondeterminism, where simulation results change with every run. Because ROS 2 uses asynchronous publish-subscribe communication, variations in scheduling and execution times alter the exact sequence of messages that callbacks receive. This makes reproducing bugs and ensuring test reliability extremely time-consuming.

To solve this, the authors adopted the concept of Logical Execution Time (LET), often used in the automotive standard AUTOSAR, and brought it to ROS 2. They defined coordination rules where every component—including periodic timers and event-driven callbacks—reads inputs and writes outputs at predefined time instants. A key idea is sending an empty record even when no message is produced. Because of this, which component depends on data from which other component is completely fixed before the simulation even starts.

Once dependencies are known beforehand, the simulation does not have to advance simulation time step by step. As long as required input data is ready, components at future time instants can run in advance and in parallel (out-of-order execution). Implemented in ROS 2 without changing a single line of existing application code, this simulator achieves up to a 228x speedup over sequential execution and up to 2.6x over conventional synchronous parallel simulation on a 256-core machine.
contributions: Proposed a lightweight coordination scheme that fixes input and output instants—including for event-driven processing—and uses empty records to make ROS 2 application behavior fully deterministic across platforms.
Developed an out-of-order parallel simulation algorithm that computes dependencies on demand and executes tasks in parallel and out of order without building the entire dependency graph in memory.
Implemented the approach by loading existing shared libraries directly, without modifying ROS 2 core libraries or user application code.
Demonstrated high parallel efficiency and memory efficiency across an Autoware reference system, multi-robot fleets, a stereo camera pipeline, and 1,385 synthetic graphs.

sections.heading: How Is Exactly One Behavior Guaranteed? Deterministic Semantics
sections.summary: ROS 2 nodes and communication are modeled as a directed graph, with fixed computation and communication delays assigned to all tasks. Sending empty records when there is no data fixes which tasks activate and when before the run.
sections.details:
### II-A System Model
A ROS 2 application is modeled as a directed graph $G=(V, E)$. The vertices $V$ represent callback functions, which are either periodic timer callbacks (time-driven) or subscription callbacks triggered by message arrival (event-driven). All callbacks and member variables within a single node are grouped into a task $\tau_i$, whose internal state $s_i$ can only be updated by callbacks within that task.

### II-B Execution Semantics
The core of achieving determinism is decoupling computation and communication. Each task $\tau_i$ is assigned a fixed computation delay $D_i$, and each communication channel $e$ is assigned a fixed transport delay $\delta_e$. A job created by an activated callback always reads its inputs at its activation instant. Regardless of when actual computation finishes, it commits its outputs at a write instant that is exactly $D_i$ after its activation.

A crucial mechanism here is the "empty record." Even when a condition dictates that no message should be sent, an empty record is transmitted. Because the transport delay $\delta_e$ is also fixed, downstream event-driven callbacks are guaranteed to activate at deterministic instants. If an empty record is received, the callback skips processing while keeping its internal state intact, propagating an empty record to downstream channels.

### II-C Determinism Guarantee
Under these rules, which job activates at which instant and which record written by which job it reads are uniquely determined solely by node function definitions, periods, and delay parameters. Completely independent of CPU load, scheduling order, or hardware differences, exactly the same output behavior is always produced for identical inputs.

### II-D Dependencies Form an Acyclic Graph
Thanks to empty records, dependencies between jobs can be determined before the simulation runs without inspecting computation outcomes. A job depends only on two things: the previous job of the same task (state handover) and the job that wrote its input message (data delivery). Even if communication topics form cycles between nodes, the job-level dependencies always form a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

sections.heading: Running Ahead of Time: Out-of-Order Parallel Simulation
sections.summary: Because job dependencies are fixed beforehand as a DAG, future simulation jobs can run ahead in parallel as soon as their inputs are ready. This combines on-demand dependency calculation using streams with memory capping via ring buffers.
sections.details:
### III-A Activation Streams
Processing jobs in topological order according to their dependencies yields correct results even when executed out of order across simulation time. However, building a dependency graph for millions of jobs in memory causes high overhead. To avoid this, periodic job chains are grouped into "activation streams." Starting from root streams for time-driven callbacks, child streams branch out in a tree structure offset by delays. By comparing job keys (activation time and priority rank), dependencies can be checked on the fly without constructing a graph in memory.

### III-B Ring Buffers to Cap Memory Usage
If upstream producers run far ahead and write future messages, unconsumed messages can exhaust memory. To prevent this, each stream manages its output records in a fixed-slot ring buffer. To overwrite and reuse a slot, a new dependency (slot dependency) is added: all child jobs that read older data in that slot must have completed. By introducing a formula to compute an appropriate slot count $K_\sigma$, the buffer size is minimized without causing deadlocks (cyclic waits).

### III-C Parallel Execution Algorithm with Worker Threads
A thread pool handles execution, managing the next runnable job of each task in a heap tree. Workers use atomic Compare-And-Swap (CAS) operations to pick up jobs without duplication, balancing load via work-stealing (idle workers stealing tasks from other workers' queues). Once a job completes, any dependent downstream jobs are immediately pushed to the ready queue.

sections.heading: Zero Code Changes: How It Integrates with ROS 2
sections.summary: By replacing ROS clock and communication functions in the C library (rcl) directly beneath the C++ client library (rclcpp), existing applications can run without code modifications or recompilation.
sections.details:
### Integration Design with Zero Application Changes
In robotics, developers want to avoid rewriting application code just for simulation. This approach leverages the standard layered architecture of ROS 2.

In ROS 2, the C++ library `rclcpp` calls the lower-level C library `rcl`, which in turn interfaces with middleware such as DDS. The simulator overrides (via symbol resolution) the message publishing and ROS clock functions provided by `rcl`. Worker threads invoke node callbacks directly. When a node queries the current time, the simulator returns that job's logical activation instant. When a node publishes a message, it is serialized directly into a slot in the simulator's ring buffer.

### Minimizing User Effort
Users do not need to manually write a directed graph model. At startup, the simulator discovers the timers and subscriptions in each node, automatically constructing the connection graph based on topic names and types. All the user needs to provide is a configuration file specifying computation and transport delays for each task.

sections.heading: Performance: Up to 228x Speedup on 256 Cores
sections.summary: Performance was evaluated on an autonomous driving reference system, a multi-robot fleet, stereo vision, and 1,385 synthetic graphs. The simulator ran up to 2.6x faster than synchronous parallel simulation and used an order of magnitude less message memory than asynchronous parallel simulation.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on a machine equipped with two AMD EPYC 9755 processors (256 cores total). Benchmarks included the Reference System (RS) based on the Autoware autonomous driving software, "Fleet-N" scaling RS across multiple vehicles, a "Stereo" camera pipeline, and 1,385 diverse synthetic graphs. Baselines included sequential execution (single-threaded), synchronous parallel approaches that pause at time boundaries (Sync-I, Sync-W), and an asynchronous parallel approach (Async) using optimistic/conservative advancement.

### V-B Speedup and Scalability
In Fleet-64 simulating 64 vehicles (1,600 nodes, ~560,000 jobs), sequential execution took 228 seconds, while the proposed method finished in just 1.0 second with 256 workers. This corresponds to a 228x speedup, achieving 91% of the theoretical limit (252x) derived from the critical path length. It was also 2.6x faster than Sync-W (89x speedup), which synchronizes threads with barriers at each time window. In Sync-W, all workers wait for the heaviest job in a window to finish, whereas the proposed method avoids idle time by computing future jobs ahead of time.

### Memory Footprint and Synthetic Graphs
While the asynchronous parallel method (Async) achieves comparable execution speeds, producers running ahead accumulate unconsumed messages. In the Stereo pipeline, Async required up to 6.3 GB of message memory. In contrast, the proposed method capped memory at 0.5 GB using ring buffers—more than a 12x reduction. In the 1,385 synthetic graph experiments shown in Fig. 5(a), the proposed method was 1.98x faster than Sync-W on geometric mean, proving robust and high parallel efficiency across a wide variety of graph structures.

captions.F5: Fig. 5: (a) Speedup comparison between the proposed method and the synchronous parallel baseline (Sync-W) across 1,385 synthetic graphs with 32 workers. Even as the number of jobs per window (x) increases in Sync-W, the proposed method consistently outperforms it, achieving roughly a 2x geometric-mean speedup.

sections.heading: How Does It Differ from Existing Deterministic Approaches?
sections.summary: Logical Execution Time (LET) originated in automotive embedded systems, but primarily targeted periodic tasks. Extending LET to event-driven processing via empty records and running out of order without barrier synchronization are unique to this work.
sections.details:
### Relationship to Automotive Systems and LET
In real-time systems, Logical Execution Time (LET) and AUTOSAR coordination techniques abstract execution time by fixing input and output instants. However, these primarily targeted periodic, time-driven tasks and were difficult to apply directly to event-driven message passing in ROS 2. This paper extends LET's deterministic guarantees to event-driven callbacks by introducing "empty records."

### Differences from Existing Deterministic ROS 2 Simulators
Prior efforts to address ROS 2 nondeterminism include advancing a virtual clock on a single thread, orchestrator-based approaches that arbitrate message delivery orders, and mappings to coordination languages like Lingua Franca based on the Reactor model. However, because they cannot know in advance whether a job will produce a message, they generally rely on synchronous execution where all components align at discrete time steps. This paper sets itself apart by using empty records to fix dependencies beforehand, unlocking barrier-free, out-of-order parallel execution across simulation time.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Work
sections.summary: By fixing I/O instants and introducing empty records, deterministic and ultra-fast out-of-order parallel simulation for ROS 2 applications was realized. Future work includes handling dynamic changes in node topologies.
sections.details:
This paper showed that fixing callback read and write instants makes ROS 2 applications fully deterministic, and that empty records allow dependencies to be known before execution. Leveraging this property, the out-of-order parallel simulator achieved remarkable scaling, reaching 91% of the theoretical speedup limit on 256 cores.

Current limitations include cases where multiple publishers within the same node write to the same topic, and graphs where topic connections change dynamically during runtime. Addressing these scenarios remains an important direction for future research.

takeaways: Explicitly transmitting the information that "nothing was produced" (empty records) fixes the dependency graph of an event-driven system as a DAG in advance, greatly increasing parallelization flexibility.
Simulation does not need to strictly follow chronological time; future jobs can run ahead out of order as long as data and state dependencies are met.
By hooking into the communication layer between rclcpp and rcl, the fast simulator integrates seamlessly without modifying existing application code or build environments.
limitations: Currently does not support configurations where multiple callbacks within the same node publish to the same topic.
Cannot handle dynamic graph structures where nodes or topics are created or destroyed during simulation.

Computation and transport delays for each task must be provided statically in a configuration file, leaving open the challenge of estimating worst-case execution times (WCET) and communication delays on actual hardware.
